newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korea woos Japan, angers U.S. Senate.
newsitem.headline: North Korea woos Japan, angers U.S. Senate.

text.p: North Korea sought to patch up stormy relations with Japan on Thursday, but drew fire from an angry U.S. Senate after its troops crossed the border into South Korea and sparked a fierce gunbattle.
The Senate voted unanimously to cut additional economic aid to North Korea if it ever repeated Wednesday's violation of its truce agreement with the South.
However, the U.S. State Department took a softer line, condemning the action as unusually provocative but insisting it would not derail food aid or efforts to bring North Korea into peace talks.

Shortly after the U.S. assurances on aid, reports from Tokyo said hunger-stricken North Korea had exported a large shipment of grain to Japan, casting uncertainty over an international relief appeal for the country.
And Pyongyang said it was lifting a ban that has prevented Japanese wives of North Koreans from leaving the communist nation to visit their homeland.
Japan welcomed the gesture, which removes a thorn in troubled relations between the two nations and could open the way to Japanese food aid.
The official Korean Central News Agency said arrangements were being made to allow the ageing women, estimated to number about 1,800, to visit Japan soon.

Most of the women married their husbands in Japan and followed them to North Korea between 1959 and 1982. But they were stranded as relations soured between the two countries, which have no diplomatic relations.
"We must welcome the North Korean announcement," Japanese government spokesman Kaoru Yosano told a news conference.

The U.S. Senate sent a sharp warning to Pyongyang over Wednesday's border clash, which began after 14 North Koreans crossed the Military Demarcation Line that runs through the middle of the Demilitarized Zone.
The buffer zone splits the Korean peninsula under an armistice agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
South Korea said Northern forces fired artillery rounds and aimed rifle and machinegun fire at Southern guard posts as part of a deliberate provocation.
North Korea said several of its soldiers were wounded in what was one of the most serious clashes in many years along the heavily fortified border.

Republican Senator Frank Murkowski won approval for an amendment to a foreign spending bill that orders the president to certify that North Korea is in compliance with the Korean armistice for nine months prior to any additional aid.
The amendment would withhold $14 million sought by the Clinton administration in fiscal 1998 to fund an international consortium supplying nuclear reactors to North Korea under a 1994 agreement.
It would not affect a $30 million contribution called for under the original terms of the accord.
In Seoul, the U.S.-led U.N. Command said it was investigating the clash, but insisted that none of the 37,000 U.S. forces in the South had been placed on a higher alert.
The Command is reponsible for monitoring the armistice.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the incident underscored the importance of starting four-way peace talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China.
Discussions aimed at setting an agenda for the talks are scheduled to begin in New York on August 5.

Burns said North Korea's action was "definitely more aggressive than usual" but would have no effect on aid. The United States announced this week it was more than doubling its food aid from $25 million to $52 million.
Meanwhile, Japanese customs officials said on Thursday 1,000 tonnes of corn from North Korea was being offloaded at a northern port.

The Japanese daily Sankei Shimbun said a poultry farmer in Yokohama ordered the grain as chicken feed through a Japan-based North Korean trading company. It estimated the cargo was worth 13 million yen ($112,000).
